summary: Specifies the news and nntp URI schemes, originally defined in RFC 1738. It was written so RFC 1738 could be made obsolete while keeping these schemes on the Standards Track.

eli5.summary: A link can point to a discussion group the way a web link points to a page. This note keeps the rules for those two older kinds of links.

questions: what is the news uri scheme
what is the nntp uri scheme
what is the snews uri scheme
how do i write a news url for a newsgroup
subtitle: How a link can point at a Usenet article or newsgroup, moved out of RFC 1738 so that RFC could retire.

tldr.problem: The 'news' and 'nntp' URI schemes were defined only in RFC 1738, which was due to be moved to historic status, and real-world use had drifted from that original text.
tldr.mechanism: This memo extracts the two schemes, updates them for modern usage, and gives their syntax in ABNF: 'nntp' names a group or article number on a specific server, 'news' names a Message-ID or a set of newsgroups with an optional server.
tldr.outcome: The IANA registry now points to this memo instead of RFC 1738 for both schemes, so the information stays on the Standards Track.

today: RFC 5538 is a Proposed Standard and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It is now the IANA reference for the 'news' and 'nntp' URI schemes, in place of RFC 1738.

sections.title: Why the Schemes Were Extracted
sections.content:
The first definition of many URI schemes appears in RFC 1738. This memo pulls out the 'news' and 'nntp' schemes so that the material can stay on the Standards Track if RFC 1738 is moved to historic status. It belongs to a series of similar documents (RFC 4156, RFC 4157, RFC 4248 and RFC 4266).

The definitions here are updates based on modern usage. The memo deliberately limits its description of 'news' to essential features that should work with any browser and any Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) server.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook for these links was about to be retired. This note copies the rules into a new book, with a few fixes, so they stay official.

sections.title: What the Two Schemes Identify
sections.content:
Both schemes identify resources on an NNTP server: individual articles, individual newsgroups, or sets of newsgroups. A user agent such as a web browser uses NNTP to fetch them. How it does so, for example with a separate or built-in newsreader, depends on the implementation. The default port for NNTP is 119.

An 'nntp' URI always names a server (it has a non-empty authority) and identifies an article by its number within a group on that server. Article numbers are local: the same article usually has a different number on another server. For that reason 'nntp' is of limited use and less widely supported.

A 'news' URI identifies an article by its worldwide unique Message-ID, independent of server and group. It can also identify newsgroups or sets of them, since a group has the same name on any server that carries it. The @ in a Message-ID is what lets a parser tell a Message-ID from a group name.
sections.eli5: An 'nntp' link is like giving a shelf number in one particular library, which differs elsewhere. A 'news' link is like naming the book by its unique title, so any library can find it.

sections.title: Syntax of 'nntp' URIs
sections.content:
An 'nntp' URI has the form nntp://server/group[/article-number]. The server is an RFC 3986 authority. The group is made of letters, digits, hyphen, plus sign, underscore and period, plus percent-encoded bytes. The article number is 1 to 16 digits.

Newsgroup names that need other characters, which NNTP allows in theory, are covered by percent-encoding. The memo gives nntp://wild.server.example/example.group.n%2Fa/12345 as an example. Without the article number, the URI names a single group, which an equivalent 'news' URL can also do and which user agents support better.
sections.eli5: It reads like a street address: which server, which group, and optionally which numbered article. Odd characters get written in a safe code.

sections.title: Syntax of 'news' URIs
sections.content:
A 'news' URI is news:[server/](article / newsgroups). If no server is given, a configured default server is used. The optional server part follows the generic authority syntax, preceded by //.

The article form is a Message-ID without angle brackets. Characters in the generic delimiters, together with %, MUST be percent-encoded; the ones that can occur in a Message-ID and must be encoded are slash, question mark, number sign, both square brackets and the percent sign itself. A consumer must decode them before passing the ID to an NNTP server.

The newsgroups form is an NNTP wildmat pattern, a group name with wildcards asterisk and question mark. Any ? must be written %3F. RFC 1738 offered only a single asterisk for all groups. With wildcards, user agents may list matching group names; without them, the URI names one group.

Query parts are not specified for either scheme, there are no special . or .. path segments, and a Message-ID without angle brackets is treated as case-sensitive.
sections.eli5: A 'news' link either holds an article's unique label or a group name that may contain wildcard symbols, like asking for every book whose title starts a certain way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and the Historic 'snews'
sections.content:
The IANA registry of URI schemes was updated to point to this memo instead of RFC 1738 for 'news' and 'nntp'.

The memo also registers the historical 'snews' scheme. It is syntactically the same as 'news' but means NNTP over SSL/TLS on port 563 (registered as 'nntps'). It was not widely deployed, and further use is deprecated in favor of ordinary 'news' URLs with servers that support RFC 4642.

Finally, the MIME news-message-ID access type, wrongly listed as a subtype, was moved to the access types registry. The memo reproduces the definition from RFC 1849 so the registry has an RFC to cite.
sections.eli5: The official list of link types now points to this note. An old, rarely used secure version of the link is recorded as retired.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
NNTP may send passwords in the clear or offer no privacy, which is considered extremely unsafe. RFC 4642 and RFC 4643 discuss alternatives. The user:password form of userinfo in the authority is deprecated by RFC 3986.

Articles on servers typically expire, so URLs may stop working. A Message-ID is supposed to be globally unique, but NNTP does not guarantee it, so attackers could try to distribute malicious content under a known URL. A URI that does not match the generic syntax is invalid.

For internationalization, the schemes were updated to allow percent-encoded UTF-8 in newsgroup names, although the Netnews article format does not yet allow UTF-8 there.
sections.eli5: Old news servers can be nosy and forgetful: they may not hide secrets, and old links can go dead or point at something different later.
